Horizon Commerce · Brand Marketing Mode Strategy Brief · Meta + Google · Confidential · 2026-06-14

The opportunity is one story across two platforms.

A cross-platform read for Bob's Discount Furniture — Meta paid social plus Google Ads Transparency Center (search/text + display image ads). Where each brand shows up, what their Google text ads actually promise, and whether the message holds across channels.

Window: Meta ads as of 2026-06-14; Google Ads Transparency Center captured 2026-06-14. Subject: Bob’s. Set: Ashley, Rooms To Go, Raymour & Flanigan, Value City, American Freight, Wayfair.

Method note: the Google panel is a captured sample — the most-surfaced ~40 creatives per advertiser from the Ads Transparency Center (image/Shopping, text/search, and video formats), with text and image creatives classified the same way Meta creatives are. Treat Google counts as a sample, not a spend estimate; treat the Google message mix (what they promise, how hard they discount) as real. This is the companion to the Meta-only read — same brands, second channel.

01 · The Read

The one-line read

On Meta, the category-wide truth was that nobody is making anyone feel anything — the offer table was empty and everyone coasted on evergreen brand equity. Google tells a more uncomfortable story: the offer table is not empty on search — Bob’s just isn’t at it. Wayfair and Rooms To Go run disciplined, dated, percentage-off promo against high-intent search demand; Bob’s runs the same warm, evergreen brand voice it runs on Meta. That’s admirable consistency and a real exposure at the same time.

02 · What We See

Where each brand actually shows up

The most important cross-platform fact is that presence is not symmetric. Reading Meta volume against Google presence reorders the set:

Brand Meta ads (in set) Google (sampled) Google format skew
Rooms To Go 679 active text-led (search)
Wayfair 324 active balanced image + text
Bob’s 215 active text + image, light video
Raymour & Flanigan 61 active video-led
Ashley 13 active video-led (heavy)
American Freight 7 active almost all text/search
Value City 0 active text + image

Two brands change character completely once you add the second channel:

  • Value City was effectively invisible on Meta (zero ads in the set) — and is plainly active on Google. Its paid presence lives on search + Shopping, not paid social. Any “Value City is dormant” conclusion drawn from Meta alone is wrong; it’s just fishing in a different pond.
  • American Freight looked thin on Meta (7 ads) but is running a heavy text/search program — nearly its entire Google footprint is search ads. For a credit-tight value buyer who is actively searching (“furniture no credit check,” “same day delivery”), that’s the right channel, and AF is there.

Ashley and Raymour, quiet-ish on Meta, are video-led on Google (YouTube/display) — a brand-format play, not a search-intent play. Bob’s and Wayfair are the two that show up substantively in both channels and in both formats.

03 · The Map

What the Google text ads actually promise

This is the part the Meta read couldn’t see, and it’s the most decision-useful slice. Across the captured search/text ads, classified per headline and description:

Brand Text ads On-sale Dominant offers
Wayfair 17 13 % off, free shipping
Rooms To Go 29 19 % off, free shipping, financing
Value City 26 9 % off, financing
American Freight 30 7 % off
Bob’s 20 2 free shipping
Raymour & Flanigan 13 3 $ off / % off (light)

The split is stark. Wayfair and Rooms To Go treat Google search as a promo channel — roughly three-quarters and two-thirds of their captured text ads carry an actual stated discount, and they reach for percentage-off plus free-shipping defaults. Bob’s treats Google search the way it treats Meta — as brand real estate. Only 2 of 20 captured Bob’s text ads state a sale; the rest are brand-and-value framing: “It’s not a sale, it’s Bob’s,” “Top-rated AND affordable — Shop Bob’s in-store,” “In-stock. Delivered fast,” “Bedroom sets under $600.” The loudest concrete promise Bob’s makes on search is free shipping, not a markdown.

That is the same evergreen discipline the Meta read praised — and it carries the same cost. On Meta, evergreen is defensible because most furniture buyers aren’t in-market in a given week (Ehrenberg-Bass mental-availability logic). On search, the audience is in-market by definition — they typed the query. Showing a high-intent searcher a brand-equity line while Wayfair shows them “20% off + free shipping” is where the consistency stops being free.

04 · The Opening

Does the Bob’s message hold across platforms?

Yes — and that’s the genuinely good news. The cross-platform corpus reads as one coherent brand:

  • Meta: “Top-rated AND affordable,” $799 Consumer-Reports-recommended mattress, lifestyle-forward creative, editorial/creator partnerships.
  • Google text: “Top-rated AND affordable — Shop Bob’s in-store,” “It’s not a sale, it’s Bob’s,” value-anchored price points (“Bedroom sets under $600”).
  • Google image/Shopping: product-forward but tasteful — the captured Shopping creatives skew lifestyle-styled room shots and clean studio sets, not the bare white-background product grid the value tier usually defaults to.

The wedge — quality-validated value with more taste than the price point predicts — is intact in both channels. Bob’s is not saying different things in different places, which is rarer than it sounds in this set (Rooms To Go’s Meta presence is polluted by impersonator pages while its Google search program is clean and promo-disciplined — two completely different faces).

05 · The Push

Whitespace, now that there are two channels to see it in

1. Bob’s is under-promoting exactly where intent is highest. The recommendation from the Meta read — run one real, dated tentpole between now and July 4 — is sharper on Google. A dated “Summer Kickoff” offer surfaced on brand + category search terms would land against an audience that is actively shopping, in a channel where Bob’s currently brings a brand line to a price fight. This is the lowest-risk place to test urgency because search intent converts.

2. Free shipping is Bob’s one concrete search promise — make it louder or replace it. If free shipping is the wedge, it should be the headline, not buried. If it isn’t differentiating (Wayfair defaults to it too), Bob’s needs a second concrete promise on search — financing terms, in-stock/fast-delivery (already in the copy and underused), or a price-point hook like the “$600 bedroom” line that tested into the captured set.

3. Match Value City and American Freight on intent capture, not on social. The brands closest to Bob’s price tier are competing on Google search, sometimes invisibly to a Meta-only view. A competitive read that stops at paid social will systematically under-count them.

4. Bob’s Shopping creative is a quiet strength — fund it. The captured Google image ads are more lifestyle-styled and on-brand than the value tier norm. That’s the same “more taste than the price predicts” advantage the Meta creative shows. It’s working; it deserves budget and a tighter tie to the in-store/regional-growth story the Meta read flagged as under-told.

Positioning read

Bob's owns the value-with-validation wedge unambiguously — the hero pairs a Consumer Reports Recommended badge with a specific $799 mattress price and the conjunction 'AND' doing strategic work between 'Top-rated' and 'affordable.' This is the clearest single positioning statement of any homepage in the Bobs competitive set, and it's executed in the hero, not buried in a brand-story page.

What works
  • Names the wedge explicitly — 'Top-rated AND affordable' is the clearest single positioning sentence in the entire competitive set, with a Consumer Reports badge proving it in the same viewport
  • Brand voice extends into product UGC ('Bob, unplugged 😎', 'Did I make this Modular Bob® dog bed because it's CUTE?!') — the Bobs mascot personality is alive in customer review captions, not just in legacy ads
  • Financing call-out is warm rather than transactional ('Why wait? Bob's has flexible financing!') — softens what is usually the most utilitarian module on furniture sites
What it misses
  • Zero urgency or time-bound offer — the $799 mattress is evergreen, no Father's Day or July 4 anchor, no end-date
  • Bob himself is absent from the hero — the mascot lives in the financing banner and review UGC but not the lead viewport, missing the most distinctive brand asset
  • The four simultaneous new-store opening flights running in paid Meta (Pineville, Spartanburg, University City, Greenville) don't appear on the homepage — owned channel and paid channel aren't telling the same growth story
Design notes
  • Consumer Reports badge above the price is a credibility moat — only brand in the set borrowing third-party validation in the hero
  • Financing banner uses Bob's mascot energy (man with piggy bank) — most personality-driven below-the-fold module in the set
  • Deliver-to zip code in utility nav — implicit logistics promise, no other set member surfaces this

Positioning read

Raymour runs the most operationally sophisticated homepage in the set — tiered savings, in-stock delivery promise (3 days), 72-month financing math made explicit ($15/mo × 72 = $1,049), service channels surfaced everywhere (chat, phone, design consult). The brand is positioning itself as the most service-rich operator, with savings math that rewards bigger baskets. Not warm, but competent.

What works
  • Tiered discount math is a sophisticated lever — incentivizes bigger baskets without doing a flat blanket promotion
  • 3-day delivery promise on in-stock is the operational moat the brand is building, surfaced in the hero rather than buried in shipping FAQ
  • Free Design Consultation as a utility-nav entry treats the design phase as a service the brand provides — same upstream-audience play as TimberTech's 'For Architects' nav
What it misses
  • Three offers competing in the hero dilute each other — a single dated tentpole would out-perform the stacked tiers
  • The '80 years' trust anchor running in paid Meta isn't in the hero — heritage equity sits idle on the page
  • No emotional creative — every module is rational/operational. The 'Better Sleep Begins Here' collection spotlight is the closest to feeling, and it lives below three offers
Design notes
  • Tiered discount with explicit $ thresholds — financial reasoning treated as a feature, not hidden in fine print
  • 'In stock & delivered in 3 days or less' is a specific operational promise no peer matches in their hero
  • Financing math made explicit ($15/mo × 72 = $1,049 total, with 'in-store only with your Raymour & Flanigan Credit Account') — radical transparency on consumer credit

Positioning read

American Freight runs the deepest-value page in the entire competitive set — the hero is essentially a digital newspaper inserter ad. Multiple stacked price-point banners ($49.99, $999, $149.99) compete in the first viewport, and the brand identity sits in the price points themselves rather than in any tagline or imagery. This is positioning by repetition: lowest price, communicated relentlessly.

What works
  • Owns the lowest price-points visibly — $49.99 mattress and $99 mattress are below anything any other set member shows in their hero
  • Whole Home Package framing ($999 for everything) is competitively unique — addresses move-in / relocation buyer differently than competitors' room-by-room model
  • Location-aware top nav with store hours is operationally helpful for the audience this serves
What it misses
  • The tax-refund 'Make Every Tax Dollar Count' framing running in paid Meta in JUNE is also absent here — paid and owned are stale together
  • No financing-led messaging in the hero despite financing being the brand's competitive moat for this audience (the paid Meta 'Free Layaway / $50 down' lines don't appear)
  • Stock 'Welcome to our fashion store!' template copy in the body text suggests low homepage editorial discipline
Design notes
  • Location-aware in utility nav ('Dothan, AL · Open Today 11AM-7PM') — operational warmth in an otherwise transactional page
  • Welcome message reads 'Welcome to our fashion store!' in body text — likely CMS template copy, suggests homepage quality control is uneven
  • Red 'Every Day Hot Deals' banner anchors urgency without naming an end date — urgency-as-default rather than urgency-with-occasion
Rooms To Go
CONF 85%
Rooms To Go runs a quietly competent homepage with a brand-history essay below the fold — the strongest E-E-A-T trust play in the set — but the complete-room-package proposition that's actually their commercial differentiator is buried while a generic free-shipping line takes the hero.

Positioning read

Rooms To Go is leaning hard into a free-shipping + complete-room-package positioning. The hero is split: a navy-overlay card states the offer flatly ('SHOP, DECORATE & SAVE + FREE SHIPPING') flanked by lifestyle accent-furniture imagery. Below the fold the page becomes essentially a brand-history essay ('Family-Owned Since 1990', 'Complete Room Packages — Fast and Affordable') — unusual for a furniture homepage, suggests SEO/E-E-A-T optimization is driving content layout.

What works
  • Brand-history paragraph below the fold is a tasteful trust play — most furniture retailers hide the founding story; Rooms To Go puts it on the homepage
  • Free Shipping By Item is a clean differentiator — distinct from American Signature's 'minimum order' standard, communicated upfront
  • Region-aware delivery copy ('Find out where we offer full service furniture delivery') is honest about geographic limits rather than hiding them
What it misses
  • Hero is generic — 'SHOP, DECORATE & SAVE' is functional but not differentiated. Nobody in the set is running urgent dated offers, so this doesn't suffer competitively, but it doesn't surprise either
  • The complete-room-package story ('buy the piece, save a little; buy the room, save a lot') is buried in the brand essay below the fold — strong proposition, poor placement
  • Paid Meta is being impersonated (Novels Lover / New world publications running ads under the RTG page name) — owned channel is healthy, paid channel needs brand-protection work
Design notes
  • Body content below the fold is a brand-history essay rather than product modules — extreme SEO play (likely driven by the 'family-owned since 1990' E-E-A-T story Google rewards)
  • Rooms To Go Business Plus surfaced as a callout — most-explicit B2B-aware furniture homepage in the set after Raymour
  • Category circle-tiles with item counts ('263 items') are an unusual UX choice — surfaces breadth as a value prop
Value City
CONF 99%
Value City Furniture is out of business — the homepage is a Chapter 11 closure notice. Bob's competitive set should be redrawn around this; the geographies Value City vacated are unclaimed share for whoever moves first.
All American Signature Furniture and Value City Furniture locations are closed.
Primary CTATrack Your Order
Secondary (2)
Frequently Asked Questionshttps://www.veritaglobal.net/americansignature (Chapter 11 claims agent)
appealrationalsignaln/aleadsservicetoneshuttered
Positioning read

Value City Furniture is OUT OF BUSINESS. The homepage as captured is a Chapter 11 wind-down notice — every store closed, no returns or exchanges accepted, no gift cards honored, deposits handled via a third-party claims agent (Verita). This is not a scrape miss or a stale page; this is the current state of the brand. American Signature Inc. (the parent) has filed Chapter 11. Value City has effectively exited the competitive set.

What works
  • Clearly states closure status without burying it — material legal compliance
  • Routes claims through a single third-party authority (Verita Global) rather than asking customers to self-navigate
  • Acknowledges open commitments (financing, deposits) rather than going silent
What it misses
  • Strategically: this brand is GONE. The 'competitive set' for Bob's now has 6 active brands, not 7. Any briefing, dashboard, or strategy doc that treats Value City as a live competitor is wrong
  • There is no consumer-facing brand to analyze — positioning, messaging, design critique are all moot
  • Bob's mid-Atlantic regions where Value City previously competed are now uncontested by this brand — a real market-share opportunity worth quantifying
Design notes
  • Combined Value City + American Signature logo at top — parent and consumer-facing brands unified in the shutdown notice
  • FAQ-driven layout — every question routes to the Verita Global claims-agent URL
  • Copyright 2025 American Signature, Inc. at the footer — page has not been touched since the bankruptcy notice was posted
Capture limitations to know about
  • Captcha-blocked brands: Ashley (perimeterx), Wayfair (perimeterx) — anti-bot walls (PerimeterX, etc.) returned a challenge page instead of the homepage. No site-content analysis is possible until we route around the block.
  • Hero crop is bounded at 1500px tall — multi-fold sections below the visible hero (testimonials, FAQs, secondary product modules) are not in the homepage analysis. They are in the per-image creative taxonomy, but framed as image-only rather than as full-context site content.
  • Regional selectors block first-visit captures — Deckorators's English/Français selector and similar interstitials mean some brands' "first hero" is actually a returning-user view. The captured hero may differ from a cold visitor's experience.
  • Page-level CTA buttons aren't always in the captured images — the homepage_image taxonomy reads CTAs only when they appear inside a captured creative tile. Header / floating / sticky-bar CTAs visible on the live site can be missing.
  • Hand-authored fallback in use — the automated homepage-analysis LLM pipeline (homepage_promos via Anthropic API) is offline pending an API key. The analyses surfaced here were authored inline by Claude from direct reads of each landing_hero.png + the captured visible-text / regions / per-image taxonomy — re-runnable manually but not nightly.
  • Live A/B tests and personalization are invisible — most sites in the set run experiments. The captured hero is a single observation, not a representative sample of what every visitor sees.
Where the spend lands

Where each brand's ads are sending buyers

Every ad in the corpus carries a destination URL. Bucketed by what that URL actually is — product browse, samples, quote/lead, where-to-buy locator, brand story — this is a snapshot of where the paid social spend points. Off-brand redirects (DoubleClick measurement hops, dealer-network subdomains, opaque short-links) are surfaced honestly, not normalized away; they obscure the "true" landing distribution for any brand running heavy tracking. Dynamic Creative templates that never resolved ({site_source_name}, {ad.id}) get their own flagged bucket: a campaign-ops bug worth raising with the agency, not noise to discard. Snapshot of where ads point, not a flow analysis — no conversion or bounce signal here.
